newsitem.title: PERU: Top LatAm bankers seek ways to stabilize markets.
newsitem.headline: Top LatAm bankers seek ways to stabilize markets.

text.p: Latin American central bankers think their countries need to boost savings, prop up their banking systems and build financial safety nets to avert a return of capital flights like the one that rocked the area two years ago.

"There is a need for a robust banking system through mechanisms such as, among others, better banking supervision and setting up a fund to guarantee deposits," Bank of Spain's Deputy Governor Miguel Martin said.
"Very few countries in Latin America have these kind of mechanisms," he told Reuters during a break of a two-day central bankers meeting that wound up late Thursday.
Venezuela's Central Bank Governor Antonio Casas said two different possible mechanisms were discussed in informal talks behind closed doors.
One was establishing guarantees for depositors in case their banks run into trouble.

The other, a proposal presented informally by Venezuela to several central bankers attending the meetings, was extending the Bogota-based Latin American Reserve Fund (FLAR) -- which now comprises only five Andean nations -- to the whole region.

Casas told Reuters all central banks could contribute funds to the FLAR, currently holding only some $600 million, and use them in case of major financial disruptions such as the December 1994 Mexican peso devaluation, which jolted most Latin nations.

Argentina, one of the countries worst hit by the capital flight that hit the region after the "Tequila effect" of the Mexican devaluation, has since set up a $6.0 billion contingency fund with commercial banks.
Under the deal, banks agree for a fee to provide Argentina with an emergency fund at relatively low, pre-set interest rates in case of financial emergency.
Casas said the FLAR could be used for similar purposes, but would involve regional central banks rather than commercial institutions.
El Salvador's deputy central bank governor Gino Bettaglio said there was also widespread concern about the low level of savings in the region.
"That is a big problem throughout Latin America with the exception of Chile," he told Reuters.

Chile's savings, mostly through its private pension funds system, are about 24 percent of its gross domestic product -- double that of most countries in the region. Several Latin countries are now following in the steps of Chile and adopting private or mixed pension funds systems.
The informal central bankers meetings are a forum for frank discussions and no decisions are made, neither do they tie member countries to adopt any resolutions.
The Lima conference consisted of two separate meetings -- one of central bankers from the Americas and another of central bankers from Latin America and Spain.

The central bankers from the Americas meet every year and those from Latin America and Spain every six months. U.S. Federal Reserve Governor Susan Phillips and Bank of Canada's Deputy Governor Tim Noel attended the meetings. Officials from Germany's Bundesbank also took part as observers.

Latin American participants said they agreed that more transparency and fluidity in the banking system were necessary to boost investors' confidence and improve efficiency, which should eventually lead to lower interest rates.
They also said more trans-national cooperation and exchange of information were necessary in an era in which markets are going global.

"This should help financial systems to be more solid and stable and avoid situations like that of Mexico (whose devaluation) hit Argentina and other countries in the area," Uruguay's Central Bank President Humberto Capote said.
The fight against inflation is taking price rises to single-digit levels in most nations in an area where recently several of them were suffering from hyperinflation.
"I see solid and credible macro-economic policies to control inflation," Noel told Reuters.
Peru's, for example, was more than 7,000 percent in 1990 before President Alberto Fujimori adopted a free-market path that became the hallmark of Latin American economies in the 1990's.
Venezuela, with 103 percent inflation in 1996 -- by far the highest in Latin America -- was the one exception to the rule.
But the government has set up a target of 30-35 percent for this year and Casas said that inflation control will be Venezuela's "predominant goal".

In a speech to the bankers, Fujimori promised to press on with tough austerity policies, which also helped his government rebuild foreign reserves to a healthy $9.3 billion now from $105 million in the red when he took office.

The adoption of similar policies put an end to 10 years of negative growth in Latin America, which went down in economic annals as "The lost decade" and ushered in a new era when foreign direct investment and capital flows returned to the region. But the Tequila effect convinced bankers that a series of steps were necessary to cushion their economies.
((-- Lima newsroom, 511 221-2134))
